title: [Microsoft Azure] Introducing Azure Catalyst agentic modernization and new AI infrastructure innovations
summary: As AI continues to reshape how every business builds, operates, and competes, it is rapidly emerging as the defining workload in the cloud. This new class of agents, more demanding, complex, and dynamic than anything before them, is rewriting the rules of cloud infrastructure. Reasoning across multi-agent systems, drawing on rich context, acting in real time, and running continuously, they ask more of every layer of the platform beneath them. This week, we’re introducing innovations across Microsoft Azure that set a new standard for how the cloud powers AI: expanded AI core capabilities in Azure to build what’s next, and Azure Catalyst, an intelligent agent-led solution to modernize the apps, data, and infrastructure that already run the business. For years, we have been reengineering every layer of Azure for the unique demands of AI and proving it on the world’s most advanced AI workloads, from leading frontier models to our own GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft 365. That work has forged Azure into a single, co-engineered system, with models, silicon, and cloud infrastructure tuned as one and value compounding at every layer. This week, we take that even further. Explore Microsoft Azure New capabilities across isolated execution, agent networking, context management, and inference efficiency deliver faster, more secure agents with better unit economics. Every innovation rests on an open foundation, giving customers the freedom to run open models and open systems everywhere they operate. There is a wave of new AI applications scaling in production, and years of existing apps and data are moving to the cloud, becoming AI-ready. Azure was built for this moment. Of everything we’re announcing this week, three areas matter most: Building the next generation of AI applications. Silicon, compute, storage, and networking work as one system across Azure for inference, training, and agents. A new connected path from Microsoft Foundry to Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) gives you choice in how and where you run AI. Modernizing apps and data with agents. Azure Catalyst uses AI agents to modernize applications, data, and infrastructure in a fraction of the time and cost of traditional methods, turning decades of technical debt into the fastest path to AI. Extending AI wherever you operate. Azure Local, flex nodes for AKS and Microsoft Foundry extend AI across cloud and distributed environments, governed through Azure Arc. Windows Server 2028, now in public preview, and Windows PCs, bring AI closer to applications, data, and users, providing the choice to meet workload-specific data, performance, regulatory, and cost needs. Build and run the next generation of AI applications Microsoft Foundry and AKS are at the center of how you build and run AI from Foundry’s managed experience, to the deep customization of AKS across models, runtimes, performance, security, and infrastructure. The connected path between them runs from building AI applications and agents to running them at scale. Open-weight models and agents move seamlessly from Foundry to AKS clusters, deployed from cloud to edge, with consistent infrastructure, security policies, and governance. Learn more about Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Underneath these experiences, AI applications are challenging infrastructure in new ways: writing and executing code autonomously, connecting dynamically to multiple agents, models, tools, and data, and carrying context across long-running tasks. We’re advancing the infrastructure to meet each of these demands: Isolation and confidentiality. With the Agent Sandbox extension for AKS, agent-generated code runs in secure, managed sandboxes with virtual machine (VM)-level isolation for every session, pre-warmed pools for fast startup, and a serverless option with no infrastructure to manage. Azure confidential computing extends protection to sensitive data and workloads while in use. Agent networking and security. With Agent Grid, agents securely connect to other agents, models, tools, data, and Azure services through authenticated, encrypted connections. Identity-driven policies and default-deny network isolation control how agents communicate and what resources they can access. Context and state. Long-context, long-running agents reuse processed prompt context instead of recomputing it on the GPU, so long tasks run faster and cost less. That cached context stays durable and controlled, by you, in your Azure tenant. And we’re making Azure itself more intelligent, building in new workload-aware capabilities that combine deep context for what each AI application requires with what only the platform delivers: GPU and VM performance, topology, and real-time availability across the fleet. AKS AI Manager translates what each model needs into the right infrastructure, placing each deployment where the fleet has the GPU capacity to serve it best. The result is a cloud that makes every AI workload perform better, with faster responses, better economics, and optimal placement decisions. And across all of this, we’re extending our commitment to open-source, giving you transparency and access to the best innovation shaped by the community. Kubernetes, vLLM, and Ray, together with flex nodes for AKS in preview, bring greater flexibility from development through production, including supported GPU environments beyond Azure. You have the freedom to build on the best model, use the right framework, and run where your business needs it. We’re already seeing what’s possible with these innovations. Rockwell Automation is using AI in its factories to help engineers diagnose equipment issues and investigate product failures. As these applications move into production, Rockwell wants to build on what works and bring those approaches to other facilities: Running our factory-level AI applications on Azure gives us one foundation for different AI workloads in production. When something works in one plant, we can adapt it for the next instead of starting over. —Justin Litherland, Vice President, Enterprise Program Management, IT, Rockwell Automation Within our own teams, Microsoft 365 engineering built COSMIC, a shared platform on AKS, to help them ship faster with built-in security, compliance, and reliability. Making infrastructure easier to run matters for developers. COSMIC handles infrastructure centrally so developers can focus on customer experiences rather than Kubernetes operations. What we learn as our own customer continues to shape future Azure capabilities for you. To go deeper at Microsoft Ignite, check out these sessions: BRK420: Deploy and run Microsoft Foundry models and agents on Kubernetes BRK448: Run secure agent loops in production with isolated sandboxes at scale BRK429: The evolution of Azure infrastructure for AI models, apps, and agents Learn more about Microsoft Foundry Modernize applications and data with Azure Catalyst The need to modernize is universal. But with developers stretched thin, custom code and deep running dependencies, progress often stalls and the backlog keeps growing. Decades of technical debt adds security exposure, cost and complexity, while disconnected tools create friction from assessment to execution. Agents in Azure Catalyst change that, analyzing legacy code, mapping dependencies, and planning and executing with precision. Work that once took months or years can now be done in weeks or even days, even with limited resources and skills, making it possible to modernize systems that were previously out of reach. Learn more about Azure Catalyst The results are real: 1.4 million applications modernized, with businesses like Levi Strauss modernizing its enterprise systems and deploying more than 1,000 agents across them. Azure Catalyst modernizes end to end—across applications, data, and infrastructure in one solution—delivered in the tools hundreds of millions of developers and IT professionals already use. Here’s what sets it apart: One connected experience Azure Catalyst connects IT teams and developers across an end-to-end process from discovery to design and execution. New capabilities add rich estate insights, AI-powered application discovery, modernization strategy and cost comparisons, and AI-generated migration waves. Execution spans applications, containers, storage, networking, and databases, and builds on existing coverage for Java and .NET modernization and migration support for VMware, Hyper-V, and physical servers. Tailored to your business Governance rulebooks and bring-your-own-model support let you set the standards, guardrails, and models agents follow, so plans fit your architecture, priorities, and security requirements. Reusable runbooks and skills make what works repeatable, so every project meets your exact standards. Secure from the start Outdated applications and data increase security exposure. Azure Catalyst works with Microsoft Security to find, prioritize, and eliminate vulnerabilities end to end. Together they scan and rank risk, prioritize actions by severity and exposure, and flag vulnerable code and databases for modernization. Through GitHub Copilot you can quickly remediate vulnerabilities as applications are modernized, fixing them once and shipping as both modern and hardened. Ready for AI Azure Catalyst works in GitHub Copilot to help teams understand the business logic and dependencies of complex applications and upgrade those apps to run on Azure’s managed services. These upgrades make it easier to connect apps to AI workflows. New previews support modernizing applications and databases together and migrating from BizTalk to Azure Logic Apps. And because Azure Catalyst is built for Azure, it optimizes performance, security, and economics along the way. Microsoft is customer zero for agent-led modernization, putting the same agentic tooling in Azure Catalyst across our estate. Microsoft Quantum and Xbox achieved 80% faster app modernization, while Intune upgraded a key library 75% faster than anticipated. GitHub ported the GitHub Copilot agentic harness—800,000 lines of production code—from TypeScript to Rust. By using these technologies ourselves, we learn firsthand what it takes to modernize complex, production-scale systems, from targeted fixes to large-scale code transformation, and apply those lessons to help you modernize your own environment. For a full breakdown, read the Azure Catalyst announcement blog. To go deeper at Microsoft Ignite, check out these sessions: BRK412: Rethink modernization end to end with agents BRK409: Modernize faster with AI-powered discovery, planning, and execution BRK410: Accelerating Java, .NET, and database modernization with agents Read more about Azure Catalyst in this blog Run AI across cloud, edge, and devices Across cloud, enterprise infrastructure, edge, physical systems, and personal devices, we’re giving you the power to run AI where your business needs it. Azure Local and flex nodes for AKS extend cloud infrastructure and Kubernetes compute into distributed environments, while extending Microsoft Foundry across these environments. Azure Arc provides consistent infrastructure management and governance end to end. New at Microsoft Ignite, Windows Server 2028 enables AI inference alongside business-critical applications and data, while Windows PCs bring intelligence directly to the devices where people work through local processing. Together, you compose the right infrastructure for each AI workload to best meet data, performance, regulatory, and cost requirements. For a full breakdown, read the Windows Server 2028 blog. To go deeper at Microsoft Ignite, check out these sessions: BRK418: What’s new and what’s next for Windows Server BRK442: Build sovereign AI with Azure Local and Foundry Local Read more about Windows Server 2028 in this blog Innovate on an open foundation for what comes next The architecture decisions you make today will carry your business for the next decade. Our job is to ensure the systems you depend on now can evolve into an AI-powered future, and that everything you build next runs on an open, co-engineered platform with choice over your models and where your workloads run. The real test of everything we’re introducing is how these solutions perform in your environment. We’ll keep listening and building alongside you. This week, I’m looking forward to Mark Russinovich, Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (dCISO), and Technical Fellow, Microsoft Azure and Pavan Davuluri, Executive Vice President, Windows and Devices, discussing why Azure and Windows are the foundation for mission-critical AI, from datacenters to the edge to a billion devices, at INV643: AI infrastructure from cloud to edge. title: [CNCF] Gang scheduling and topology-aware placement for AI training in Kubernetes
summary: Distributed AI training workloads impose complex scheduling requirements that Kubernetes’s built-in scheduler can’t meet. Kubernetes schedules pods individually and independently, but distributed training introduces two requirements that break this model: Pods must land on hardware with the right inter-GPU bandwidth, and all pods must be scheduled simultaneously. If either requirement goes unmet, training stalls or runs far below the hardware’s potential. Topology-aware scheduling (TAS) and gang scheduling address these two requirements and help organizations extract full value from GPU capacity, which represents a growing share of infrastructure spend. TAS shapes the relative placement of pods to enable fast communication between GPUs. Gang scheduling helps ensure that all pods in a distributed job start running simultaneously, preventing the partial starts that leave GPUs allocated but idle. Together, they give Kubernetes the placement precision and coordination that distributed workloads require. In this post, we’ll look at the scheduling problems that AI training presents for Kubernetes and how TAS and gang scheduling, implemented by Kueue and the Coscheduling plugin, solve them. We’ll explore: How the Kubernetes scheduler is unsuited for AI training How to validate gang scheduling and TAS in Kubernetes We’ll also cover the evolving capabilities of Kubernetes native scheduler to support AI training workloads. How the Kubernetes scheduler is unsuited for AI training In most batch workloads, pods operate independently. A pod can fail, be rescheduled, or be replaced with no effect on the rest of the workload. The Kubernetes scheduler handles this model well by placing pods one at a time on any eligible node without coordinating across pods. But the pods in an AI training workload are interdependent. They need to be placed on hardware with appropriate inter-GPU bandwidth, and they all need to start simultaneously. The following sections explain these requirements and how Kueue and Coscheduling address them by augmenting Kubernetes’ scheduling capabilities. How topology placement affects distributed AI training performance The physical interconnections between nodes are a key factor in the performance of AI training workloads. In each step of the training process, workers exchange data through collective communication operations, and the type and frequency of those operations depends on the job’s parallelization strategy. In pure data-parallel (DDP) training, one AllReduce operation per step aggregates, averages, and distributes gradients—the computed signals that indicate how the model’s parameters should be adjusted to improve its predictions. In large-scale training strategies that shard the model across workers, those workers instead exchange data continuously throughout a step, by using operations like gather, reduce, and all-to-all. These large-scale strategies include tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism, which are often combined in LLM pretraining. Whichever pattern a job uses, the underlying constraint is the same: This communication is latency-sensitive, and where those workers land in the cluster determines how much of that latency the job absorbs. The bandwidth available between workers depends on where they sit relative to each other in the cluster. The following topology domains are common in GPU clusters: Same node: This is generally the lowest-latency option. When the GPUs are connected by NVLink and NVSwitch, workers can use NVIDIA’s high-bandwidth GPU interconnect. Otherwise, same-node GPU communication may traverse Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) connections. Different nodes in the same rack: Workers communicate via high-speed network fabric. Cross-node traffic travels through PCIe to the network interface and back, with intermediate latency. Different racks: This is the highest-latency option. Workers communicate across the cluster’s InfiniBand fabric, which is the lowest-bandwidth hop in the path and adds further latency on top of the cross-node PCIe path. Different workloads have different tolerances for latency. In a pretraining job that comprises a large number of workers, each step blocks until the slowest worker completes its share of that step’s collective communication. Any cross-rack latency here compounds quickly, reducing effective GPU utilization. A small fine-tuning job involves fewer workers exchanging smaller gradients, so the same cross-rack penalty represents a much smaller fraction of each step’s total time. Without topology awareness, the Kubernetes scheduler places workers on any eligible nodes, regardless of their physical relationships in the cluster. The gang assembles and the training job runs, but communication overhead—rather than computation—consumes a substantial portion of each step. The job completes more slowly and at greater cost than the hardware should require. Crucially, infrastructure metrics don’t reflect this inefficiency because they measure activity, not productivity. Nothing looks wrong from an infrastructure perspective, but training throughput remains low relative to what the hardware should deliver. Kueue closes part of this gap through topology-aware placement. It groups nodes into domains—block, rack, and host—based on topology labels applied to those nodes (for example, topology.kubernetes.io/rack). Kueue places a job’s pods within a single domain that satisfies its bandwidth requirements. But Kueue doesn’t discover cluster topology on its own. The labels that define each domain have to be applied to nodes first, typically by a cluster administrator or a cloud provider’s topology labeler. Kueue enforces this placement decision at admission time. It’s an open source Kubernetes-native job queuing system that sits above the kube-scheduler, controlling which jobs reach the scheduler and when. During that admission check, it also verifies that a job’s pods fit within a topology domain. It evaluates each job against quota, priority, and preemption criteria and decides whether to allow the job to proceed. It tracks that decision in a Kueue Workload object, which represents the resource requirements, admission status, and pod sets for a job. Kueue also provides optional life cycle management for admitted jobs, including evicting and requeueing workloads whose pods don’t all reach a ready state within a configured timeout. When Kueue admits a job to be scheduled (by setting spec.suspend: false, allowing the Job controller to create pods), it writes scheduling constraints into the training job’s pod templates based on the placement mode and topology assignment it selected. Those constraints restrict which nodes the Kubernetes scheduler may assign so that pods stay within the selected topology domain. The following diagram shows the path that a pod takes from job submission to binding. Kueue acts first, writing topology constraints at admission time and clearing the job for scheduling. The Job controller creates the pods, but they exist only as objects in etcd, without assigned nodes or running containers. Coscheduling acts second, holding each pod in a waiting state until the full gang is ready to bind simultaneously. How to validate gang scheduling and TAS in Kubernetes Kueue and Coscheduling address the unique scheduling requirements of AI training workloads. To operate your training jobs effectively and efficiently, you need to know that Kueue and Coscheduling are working as intended. Because tracking down scheduling failures requires piecing together signals from multiple layers of your stack, this section breaks down how to validate each step of the process: Monitor activity in the admission queue to ensure jobs are being accepted. Validate placement effectiveness to confirm jobs land in the right physical topology. Monitor Coscheduling gang assembly to catch partial starts. Confirm scheduling effectiveness with training throughput signals to tie infrastructure metrics directly to application performance. Monitor activity in the admission queue Kueue exposes OpenMetrics-formatted metrics that show whether jobs are clearing the admission queue or stalling there. kueue_pending_workloads shows queue depth broken down by status. The active status counts jobs currently waiting in the queue for capacity to open up. The inadmissible status counts jobs that Kueue has evaluated and cannot currently admit, typically because quota in the assigned ClusterQueue is exhausted, no valid topology domain exists, or a constraint can’t be satisfied. Jobs remain inadmissible until cluster conditions change. A growing inadmissible count that doesn’t clear is a sign of a configuration or capacity problem rather than normal queuing. kueue_admission_wait_time_seconds measures how long jobs wait between creation or requeue and admission. A rising p99 indicates that jobs are arriving faster than Kueue can admit them, which can be due to quota exhaustion, priority contention among many jobs, or preemption processing taking time to complete. kueue_evicted_workloads_total tracks evictions with a reason label that distinguishes the cause of each eviction. When a node fails under TAS and Kueue cannot find a replacement, it evicts the affected workload with reason="NodeFailures". A rise in this signal points to non-recoverable node loss in the assigned topology domain. A related reason, reason="PodsReadyTimeout", fires when a gang’s pods do not reach a ready state within the configured timeout. That timeout expires for many reasons, including slow scheduling, image pulls, resource pressure, or a node failure whose recovery timed out. Treat an increase as a prompt to investigate rather than proof of a single cause. Both are post-admission stability signals, separate from confirming that a workload landed in its intended topology domain. Validate placement effectiveness In addition to tracking Kueue metrics to understand admission health and eviction behavior, you can inspect the Kueue Workload object to confirm a workload’s topology assignment: kubectl -n <namespace> get workloads.kueue.x-k8s.io <workload-name> -o yaml Look for status.admission.podSetAssignments.topologyAssignment. This field lists the topology levels and domain values into which each PodSet was placed, and is the authoritative signal that TAS was applied. After you’ve confirmed the topology assignment, use GPU and network telemetry data to validate whether the hardware is delivering the performance that placement implies. Same-node GPU communication should show NVLink or other local interconnect activity when that hardware path is available. Evaluate cross-node communication by looking at PCIe activity together with network or fabric telemetry data: PCIe throughput reflects the GPU-to-host transfers required for cross-node communication, but it does not measure the network hop itself. If throughput is low despite a valid topology assignment, look for a physical infrastructure explanation, such as driver issues, hardware faults, or fabric degradation, rather than treating it as a Kueue placement failure. Hardware bottlenecks like these can surface as lower-than-expected bandwidth and slower collective communication times, not necessarily as idle GPUs, which is why infrastructure metrics can look healthy while training throughput degrades. Monitor Coscheduling gang assembly in Kubernetes The Coscheduling plugin uses a custom resource called a PodGroup to track each training gang. A PodGroup records the gang’s minimum worker requirement and current scheduling state. Pods belong to the same PodGroup when they use the same scheduling.x-k8s.io/pod-group label. You can query PodGroups with kubectl: kubectl get podgroups.scheduling.x-k8s.io --all-namespaces For more detail about a specific gang, describe the PodGroup or inspect its status: kubectl -n <namespace> describe podgroup.scheduling.x-k8s.io <podgroup-name> kubectl -n <namespace> get podgroup.scheduling.x-k8s.io <podgroup-name> -o yaml The exact columns shown by kubectl can vary by version and CRD configuration, so focus on the PodGroup’s spec and status fields. spec.minMember shows the minimum number of pods required for the gang to run. spec.scheduleTimeoutSeconds, when configured, controls how long the group can wait. status.phase shows the gang’s current state, which is one of the following values: Pending: The PodGroup has been accepted but the scheduler has not allocated enough resources. Scheduling: More pods have been scheduled than spec.minMember, but the number of running pods hasn’t reached spec.minMember yet. Running: At least spec.minMember pods are running. Unknown: Some, but not all, of the required pods were scheduled. The rest can’t be scheduled (for example, due to insufficient resources), and the scheduler waits for controllers to recover them. Finished: The required pods completed successfully. Failed: At least one of the required pods has failed. You should expect a healthy gang to move from Pending or Scheduling to Running within the scheduling window you expect for that workload. If a gang remains Pending or Scheduling longer than expected, check the PodGroup events, associated pod events, and scheduler logs. A delay like this can indicate that the cluster cannot satisfy the gang’s resource requirements within the topology domain Kueue assigned, or that no available node satisfies scheduling requirements such as node selectors, taints, affinity, or resource availability. A gang stuck between Scheduling and Running with only partial placement may surface as Unknown rather than remaining in Scheduling. The Unknown phase differs from Failed, because the scheduler is still waiting on controllers to recover the unplaced pods, not reporting an outright failure. To distinguish an admission problem from a scheduler-level assembly problem, correlate PodGroup state with Kueue’s Workload status and admission metrics. If the Workload is still inadmissible, the issue is upstream of Coscheduling: Kueue has not admitted the job, so the fix is likely quota, priority, admission checks, or topology configuration. If the Workload is admitted and has a topology assignment, but the PodGroup remains Pending or Scheduling, the issue is later in the pipeline: Coscheduling and the kube-scheduler cannot assemble enough pods within the assigned placement and current cluster state. If a PodGroup reaches Failed, investigate the failed pods directly and look for common issues such as application failure, image or startup errors, or node disruption. Confirm scheduling effectiveness with training throughput signals Training frameworks are the software libraries that orchestrate distributed training, such as PyTorch, JAX, and Ray Train. Only by monitoring signals from these frameworks can you determine whether GPU cycles are producing completed training progress or being consumed by stalled communication. Ray is unique among these frameworks in its placement group model, which maps directly onto gang scheduling and gives it scheduling-aware observability. ray_placement_groups tracks the current number of placement groups by State, such as PENDING, CREATED, or REMOVED. A sustained increase in PENDING placement groups indicates that Ray is waiting for placement group resources to become available. ray_tasks tracks tasks by State, which can help show whether application work is accumulating while placement groups remain pending. When these signals rise together, Ray cannot satisfy its placement requirements. This can be a downstream effect of a Coscheduling assembly issue or a Kueue topology constraint problem rather than a simple application-layer slowdown. Other distributed training frameworks (including PyTorch DDP, Kubeflow operators, and Horovod) don’t expose metrics that directly reflect the Kubernetes scheduler’s effectiveness. These frameworks do provide indirect indicators in the form of throughput metrics, such as steps per second, samples per second, and tokens per second. A throughput drop in these metrics alongside decreasing GPU interconnect bandwidth and PodGroup timeouts suggests a scheduling root cause. PodGroup timeouts confirm that gang assembly did not complete within the expected scheduling window. Correlating those timeouts with the Kueue Workload’s topology assignment and GPU, PCIe, and network telemetry data can help determine whether placement constraints contributed to the slowdown. Native Kubernetes scheduling: How v1.35 through v1.37 address AI training requirements Kueue and Coscheduling are out-of-tree components, installed and managed separately from Kubernetes. Kubernetes is beginning to add native scheduler capabilities that address the complex scheduling requirements this post describes, but those features are still early. Kubernetes v1.35 introduced native support for gang scheduling as an alpha feature. Kubernetes v1.36 added several related alpha features for AI training workloads, including topology-aware scheduling, workload-aware preemption, and initial Job controller integration via a feature gate. Kubernetes v1.36 also added a native PodGroup API, distinct from the out-of-tree PodGroup custom resource definition (CRD) used by the Coscheduling plugin. Kubernetes v1.37 graduated gang scheduling and workload-aware preemption to beta under the GenericWorkload feature gate, which remains disabled by default. The native TAS implementation enables the kube-scheduler to understand physical cluster topology and place pods within an appropriate topology domain, such as a rack or zone, without requiring Kueue to write node affinity rules into pod templates. These native capabilities are not yet a drop-in replacement for the Kueue and Coscheduling path described in this post. Gang scheduling and workload-aware preemption reached beta in v1.37 but ship disabled by default and still lack feature parity with Kueue and Coscheduling. Topology-aware workload scheduling remains alpha. Kueue and Coscheduling remain the production path for distributed training scheduling. Their monitoring signals, including admission queue depth, gang assembly state, topology placement, and GPU throughput, map directly to the concepts the native APIs expose. Teams that build observability into the current stack will have a working baseline when they evaluate or migrate to these native capabilities. Get started with gang scheduling and topology-aware placement Monitoring distributed AI training scheduling in Kubernetes requires visibility across components that standard tooling doesn’t naturally connect: Kueue’s admission queue, Coscheduling’s gang assembly, the GPU interconnect, and the training framework. Applying a common topology tag across all of these signals helps you monitor your clusters’ gang scheduling and TAS activity and ensure that your training jobs make efficient progress. To get started, read the Kueue documentation and the Coscheduling plugin documentation. This post originally appeared on the Datadog blog, where you can read the full version, including how to monitor and troubleshoot this stack in production.

title: [Cloudflare] How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)
summary: On November 17, 2026, the security research company Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The flaw affects Java. OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle released patched builds in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update the same day, at 21:00 UTC.The vulnerability lets a remote attacker with no credentials send malformed Base64 data to a Java application and overwrite memory next to the decoded output. Calif turned that overwrite into a leak of heap memory, similar to Heartbleed, and into remote code execution. Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate in their default configurations, and post-authentication remote code execution against Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker.Cloudflare has released a new set of rules in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset designed to detect malformed Base64 input patterns associated with this vulnerability. The rules are available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans and are enabled by default with the Log action because malformed input and some benign application-specific token formats can resemble exploitation attempts. Blocking by default could therefore disrupt legitimate traffic. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the rules action to Block once they confirm it does not affect legitimate traffic. The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Java4Shell can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, like outbound TLS responses, and the only complete fix is to update the Java runtime. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get more information on how the vulnerability develops on the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.We have seen no indication so far that Java4Shell was exploited on Cloudflare infrastructure.What we know about the vulnerabilityBase64 is a common way to represent binary data as text. Java applications decode Base64 when they process authentication headers, tokens, file uploads and many network messages. To decode it faster, OpenJDK replaces frequently used code with specialized machine code, called intrinsics. On supported x86-64 processors, the Base64 intrinsic uses AVX-512 instructions to process 64 bytes at a time.The bug sits in the handwritten assembly that handles the final characters of the input. When the tail of the input contains padding characters (=) in a position where valid Base64 never places them, the routine calculates a negative output length. That invalid length turns into a full 64-byte write. For a 65-character input, made of 64 characters followed by a single =, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte output array and then writes 62 bytes past its end.Java eventually rejects the input as invalid and throws an exception. By then, the neighboring memory has already been overwritten. An application's own input validation does not help, because the corruption happens inside the decoder before the application can reject the data.The simplest trigger is 64 A characters followed by =. On OpenJDK 17, the trigger needs 128 characters followed by =, because the threshold for the fast code path is higher.Exploitation is not point-and-shoot. The overwritten bytes are mostly fixed values, and the attacker controls only where the write lands. To build a working exploit, Calif arranged the Java heap so that the overflow enlarged neighboring arrays, which gave them first a way to read heap memory and then a way to write chosen bytes. Each target application requires its own exploit chain. Calif reported developing its first working local exploit in about three hours with the help of AI agents, so we expect other attackers to build exploit chains quickly.Who is affectedJava4Shell affects a system only when all the following conditions are true:ConditionDetailsJava runtimeOpenJDK 17.0.6 or newer, including distributions built from OpenJDK: Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE and Oracle GraalVM for JDK. Check Oracle's advisory for the exact list of affected Oracle builds.Processorx86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI support, such as Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, or AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 processors are not affected.InputThe application decodes attacker-controlled Base64 data with the standard Java decoder.Many applications bundle their own Java runtime, and container images ship with a fixed Java Development Kit (JDK). Upgrading the system Java package does not update those copies, and it does not replace a Java virtual machine (JVM) that is already running. Every updated service needs a restart.Mitigate if you cannot patch right awayIf you cannot update immediately, Calif documents two JVM startup flags that remove the vulnerable code path:-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics disables hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding.-XX:UseAVX=2 disables AVX-512. Apply this flag only on x86-64 hosts. OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and will fail to start.Both flags require a restart and may reduce performance for workloads that decode large amounts of Base64. They buy time while you patch. They do not replace the update.Protect your infrastructure while you patchPatching every Java runtime takes time, especially when JDKs are bundled inside applications and container images. Cloudflare WAF can reduce your exposure while you patch. A new managed rule, available on paid plans and enabled in Log mode by default, detects the malformed Base64 input that triggers Java4Shell. For Business and Enterprise customers, WAF attack score adds a machine learning layer that scores each request for remote code execution payloads, which helps catch variations and bypass attempts that signature-based rules can miss.New managed rulesProtection for paid plans has been released as part of the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee). The rule is enabled by default with the Log action, because blocking by default could cause false positives on legitimate Base64 traffic. To review its matches, go to Security > Security Analytics > Events and filter by the rule ID. If the matches are not legitimate traffic, change the rule action to Block: go to Security > Settings, edit the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, search for CVE-2026-114938 and set the rule action to Block. Alternatively, you can follow the link to review your configuration on the Zero Wire briefing.Rule descriptionRule IDJava4Shell - Malformed Base64 Header - CVE-2026-1149385de9b20a45ea45d3841919ab4d718bf4Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Query Value - CVE-2026-11493846bb4172813e471ea62d31c02337b51dJava4Shell - Malformed Base64 Body Value - CVE-2026-114938d4dc3f71f1bc44a0811ae570e5e5836cJava4Shell - Malformed Base64 Path Segment - CVE-2026-1149380dceaf0684b54fd0b085fcfb6fd6f152Java4Shell - Malformed Base64url JWT Component - CVE-2026-1149380ddd0eb664a040779f2f19065a25d991Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 WebAuthn Value - CVE-2026-1149384fce1ea79a614c07a27348d167d74ebbWe are working on a rule for the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and will update this post when it is available.A WAF can block the exploit when the malformed Base64 arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable decoder, including:Encoded or nested data. The Base64 value may be wrapped inside another encoding or compressed format that the application unpacks before decoding.Non-HTTP protocols. Some affected products, such as the Apache Kafka broker, accept traffic over their own protocols.Outbound connections. Calif also shared a client-side exploit: a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own.Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. This includes internal traffic between services.Adding defense-in-depth with WAF attack scoreWhile the managed rule is the primary way to block malformed Base64 triggers at the edge, Cloudflare WAF Attack Score (and specifically its remote code execution sub-score cf.waf.score.rce available on Enterprise plans) can offer an additional, complementary layer of protection.Because CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) is a binary heap-corruption vulnerability, an attacker rarely achieves full, reliable remote code execution with a single 65-byte (or 129-byte) trigger string alone. On the wire, that initial trigger looks like an opaque, malformed Base64 string containing heap-corruption bytes rather than traditional web-layer injection syntax. As a result, machine learning models trained on application-layer injection patterns will not flag the raw Base64 trigger in isolation.Instead, turning a bounded JVM heap overflow into remote code execution over HTTP almost always requires a multi-stage or multi-parameter exploit chain, which creates more fingerprints that WAF Attack Score can inspect and flag, including:Heap Grooming and Triggering: To corrupt a predictable adjacent object on the JVM heap (such as a String or byte length header), attackers often send repetitive parameters or headers alongside the malformed Base64 payload to shape memory layout before triggering the out-of-bounds write.Second-Stage Payloads: Once heap corruption gives the attacker control over execution flow or object references, the exploit still needs commands, scripts, or Java gadgets to run. If an exploit chain pairs the initial heap-corruption trigger with a second-stage payload such as shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, cmd.exe, reverse-shell strings) or Java class-loading gadgets (java.lang.Runtime, ProcessBuilder, serialized object streams) tucked into another header, query parameter, or request body, cf.waf.score.rce can detect and score that secondary payload as malicious.Post-Exploitation Activity: Even if an initial heap-read or corruption request slips past edge filters, subsequent HTTP requests attempting to interact with an in-memory webshell or pass OS commands to the compromised JVM remain directly visible to WAF Attack Score.Deploy protections and patchBecause sophisticated in-memory exploits can still execute raw shellcode or manipulate bytecode without ever sending plaintext shell commands over HTTP, WAF Attack Score should be used alongside explicit Base64 rules and JVM patching.You can find more information on how to deploy Managed rules and attack score in our WAF guide, but in a nutshell:1. Set the CVE-2026-114938 rule in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro plan and above) to Block. It is enabled in Log mode by default, so review its matches in Security Events first. Use the links on the Cloudflare Zero Wire page to review your rules status.2. Layer Attack Score to get ML-based remote code execution (RCE) detection: create a custom rule blocking or challenging requests with a low RCE attack score (for example, cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans) to catch multi-stage exploit chains and post-exploitation command traffic.3. Remediate at runtime: Upgrade to patched OpenJDK builds (or set -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround) to eliminate the vulnerable AVX-512 code path entirely. Follow the OpenJDK advisory and Oracle's Critical Patch Update and install your Java vendor's fixed release as soon as possible. For a prompt you can give an AI agent to inventory your Java runtimes, see the Java4Shell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire. Impact on Cloudflare infrastructureCloudflare also runs Java, so when Java4Shell was disclosed we checked our own systems. The vulnerability can only be triggered in specific hardware configurations, namely a x86-64 processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI, so a system is exposed only when both are true. Our investigation found that the majority of our Java workloads are not scheduled on vulnerable systems; we took immediate action to protect the remainder.About an hour after the patches were published, we began rolling out a JVM startup option that turns off the accelerated Base64 routine containing the bug on all Java workloads, so decoding falls back to the standard implementation. To be safe, we are rolling out our patched configuration to all machines, regardless of hardware as a precaution. We have seen no indication so far that Java4Shell was exploited on Cloudflare infrastructure.Update every Java runtime nowJava4Shell turns a performance optimization in the Java runtime into a path to remote code execution, and with technical details now public, we expect exploit attempts to follow quickly. The fix is to update every Java runtime and restart the services that use it. While you patch, review the new managed rule's matches and switch it to Block if you are on a paid plan and use attack score to catch remote code execution payloads that signatures may miss. Our WAF analysts will continue to update protections as new techniques emerge. Follow the WAF changelog for rule updates and the Java4Shell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire for the latest on this vulnerability.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Microsoft Ignite 2026: What’s new in Azure, the platform purpose-built for AI
summary: Azure at Microsoft Ignite 2026: The headlines Azure AI core: AI on infrastructure you control. Azure Cobalt 200: Our highest-performing general-purpose virtual machines (VMs). Azure Catalyst: Agent-led modernization from plan to code. Agentic cloud operations: Agents that keep your cloud running well. Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB: PostgreSQL for AI apps and analytics. Fabric apps: Governed apps built on trusted data. Microsoft IQ: Context for every agent. Over the past year, my conversations with customers have changed. A year ago, the question was which model to choose. Now it’s how to put agents to work on the processes that run the business, and how to trust them to do it. With the same frontier models available to everyone, the advantage comes from what no one else has: your context. It’s how your business runs, what your people know, and the systems and data you’ve spent years building. That’s your IQ. It’s your intellectual property, so it should stay yours, and it should work wherever your people and agents do. Our job is to make every layer beneath your agents better, from the infrastructure that runs them and the estate they act on to the apps they power and the business context that tells them how your company works. Azure is the foundation of Frontier Transformation. We engineer Azure as one system, so the knowledge an agent needs stays governed and the security you use to protect your people extends to the agents acting for them. And because we’re evolving the open, cloud-native platform you already rely on, you don’t have to start over. See what Azure can do for your business As Satya Nadella shared at Microsoft Build in June, we added more datacenter capacity in 18 months than in Azure’s first decade. Combined with more regions than any other cloud provider, you can scale your AI workloads globally with confidence as demand grows. This week at Microsoft Ignite, we’re sharing what’s new across every layer of the platform. New capabilities spanning compute, storage, and networking let you run AI at scale with the control of your own infrastructure, without having to build, secure, and operate all of it yourself. Azure Catalyst brings agent-led modernization together in one experience from estate to code. PostgreSQL now has two homes at Microsoft: Azure HorizonDB, generally available for mission-critical scale, and the new Fabric HorizonDB, which connects your PostgreSQL apps to analytics and AI. And Fabric apps, now generally available, let your teams turn trusted enterprise data into working apps. We’re also introducing Microsoft IQ, the enterprise context management platform that helps you build your own IQ and put it to work in every app and agent. It also gives your teams a path on Azure to build, run, and continuously improve those agents. Run AI at scale with the control you choose It starts with the infrastructure that runs your agents. As they take on real work, you should be able to run them on your terms, with your choice of models, your data, and where they run. That control lets you find the right balance of performance and cost for each workload and adapt as models and needs change. But control comes with real work and risk. Platform teams end up assembling and operating much of the AI stack themselves and stretching GPUs to keep up with shifting demand. Agents that reach models, tools, and data and run code on their own open new security gaps, putting sensitive data at risk. Teams want the control of running their own AI infrastructure without taking on all the manual toil of building, securing, and operating it. Building the AI core on Azure That’s what we’re bringing to Azure. New capabilities across compute, storage, and networking come together as one AI foundation, so you keep control of your models and workloads while Azure takes on the work underneath. Build AI with Microsoft Foundry in a fully managed experience and run it at scale with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) when you need more control over performance, security, and cost. Ignite session: AI infrastructure from cloud to Edge Watch now ↗ Azure sets up and tunes the infrastructure for you, so your teams spend less time on configuration and more time moving models and agents into production. Workloads are placed based on available capacity, so your GPU investment goes further as demand grows. Security is enforced centrally across agents, models, and tools, giving security teams consistent controls wherever agents run. And because it’s built on open-source projects, your workloads stay portable, including to your own servers outside Azure, keeping your options open as your needs change. The result is AI that scales with your business, on infrastructure you control. To hear how organizations are operating AI at scale, join Mark Russinovich and Pavan Davuluri in the innovation session “AI Infrastructure from cloud to edge.” Strengthening every layer of your AI estate with Azure Cobalt 200 Agents reason, make decisions, and run continuously, and that’s reshaping what cloud infrastructure needs to deliver. That’s why we design Azure as one system, from silicon to servers to services. We pair our own Maia and Cobalt chips with the latest from NVIDIA and AMD, so every workload runs on the right silicon for the job. Our strategy focuses on building performance, efficiency, and security into every layer. The result is AI that’s faster and more economical to run at scale, on a roadmap you can plan around. Ignite session: cobalt 200… Watch now ↗ Azure Cobalt 200 virtual machines, our highest-performing general-purpose VMs, are now generally available. Designed from the ground up for scale-out, cloud native, and agentic AI workloads, these VMs deliver up to 50% better CPU performance compared to our Cobalt 100 VMs. Together with Maia, they give you an infrastructure you can plan around. Read about the latest Azure Cobalt updates in this blog Agent-led modernization and operations, from estate to code Agents are only as useful as the systems they can act on. Much of what makes your company unique is built into your applications and databases and years of business logic your teams rely on. Modernizing puts existing apps and data to work in new AI-powered experiences, helps teams ship faster, and lowers the cost and risk of running older systems, creating a more adaptable foundation for growth. Getting there isn’t easy. Modernizing can mean mapping complex systems and changing code that few people fully understand. Keeping the estate running well means sorting through constant signals with little knowledge on what matters most. And as agents take on more of that work, teams need to let them act while keeping the oversight your business requires. That’s why we’re bringing agents to both, from estate to code. Azure Catalyst helps you modernize applications, code, and databases from plan to execution. And new capabilities in Azure Copilot, Azure SRE Agent, and Azure Monitor help keep your cloud and databases running well, with people in control. Modernize for AI with Azure Catalyst Azure Catalyst is a new unified experience for agentic modernization. It brings discovery, planning, migration, modernization, and code intelligence together, so IT teams and developers work from the same plan across infrastructure, applications, and data. Azure Catalyst modernizes the technology you already have into a foundation for AI, putting the business logic in your existing applications to work in new AI-powered experiences and agentic business processes. Ignite session: rethink modernization… Watch now ↗ For IT teams, Azure Catalyst agent extends from migration planning into deeper modernization and execution. For developers, GitHub Copilot modernization carries that plan into code in the tools they already use, with agent governance rulebooks and bring-your-own-model support that customizes your modernization project to the specifications of each business. And Azure Catalyst delivers a deeper understanding of how enterprise applications work, so teams can assess the impact of changes, modernize faster, and find where legacy processes could be reimagined with AI. Ignite session: modernize faster with ai… Watch now ↗ Modernization can also close security gaps. End-of-support runtimes, unpatched dependencies, and aging code widen your threat surface. Azure Catalyst works with Microsoft Security to fix that: Microsoft Perception and MDASH rank vulnerabilities across your estate and code, Azure Catalyst identifies vulnerable code and databases to modernize first, and GitHub Copilot turns those findings into fixes in the same pass. Each app comes out more secure than it went in. Learn more about Azure AI foundation and Azure Catalyst in this blog Keep your cloud running well with agentic operations As applications scale across hybrid infrastructure, microservices, and AI workloads, leading organizations are moving to operating models where insight flows directly into action. That’s the idea behind agentic operations: AI agents, guided by your intent, continuously observe, reason, and help take action across the cloud lifecycle. Signals feed coordinated workflows that improve performance, cost, and reliability as systems run, with people kept in control. At Microsoft Ignite, we’re bringing that model to more of your estate. Azure Copilot‘s deployment agent, now generally available, helps you go from requirements described in natural language to deployed cloud workloads. You can even extend agentic operations to Oracle and SAP with Azure Workload Center, now in limited preview. Ignite session: put ai agents to work… Watch now ↗ Azure SRE Agent brings agentic operations into secure production environments, with new enterprise controls in preview, while Microsoft Entra Agent ID and Agent 365 give central teams a consistent way to discover, govern, and audit agents throughout their lifecycle. We’re also giving agents richer data and understanding so they can detect issues earlier, diagnose problems faster, and take more effective action. Azure Monitor health models, now generally available, give agents a real-time view of your application architecture and business priorities, so they can recommend fixes. Learn more about agentic operations in this blog Build the next generation of AI apps Then there are the apps your agents power, where business data becomes business value. The question for every organization is how quickly it can move from idea to an app the entire business can rely on. Today, the people building AI apps span the whole organization. Developers are creating mission-critical systems and new apps with agents, while teams across the business are describing the app they need in Copilot. Each needs something different from the platform, but every app needs to connect to business data and run under governance IT can trust. We’re building one foundation for all of them, and it starts with PostgreSQL, the database of choice for a growing share of developers. With Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB, you can run PostgreSQL wherever your apps need it, from mission-critical systems to analytics and AI. Fabric apps builds on that foundation, so teams can turn business data into working apps, whether they start in code or in conversation. Power your AI apps with PostgreSQL on Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB The apps developers build now reason over data, call models, and act for users, so the database underneath has to bring transactions, vectors, and AI together at mission-critical scale. Azure HorizonDB, now generally available, is a fully managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database built for that work. It delivers millisecond latency with built-in vector indexing, so your apps can find, reason over, and act on data in one place. Enterprise-grade security comes built in, and developers can work in tools they already know, including GitHub Copilot and Visual Studio Code. ignite session: data foundations for modern apps… Watch now ↗ We’re also extending the power of PostgreSQL directly into Microsoft Fabric. Fabric HorizonDB, now in public preview, brings a serverless, Fabric-native PostgreSQL experience alongside SQL database in Fabric and Cosmos DB in Fabric. By bringing operational databases, analytics, and AI together on a unified, governed platform, developers can build intelligent applications with less data movement and complexity. Fabric HorizonDB will also serve as the PostgreSQL backend for Fabric apps. To simplify database management across environments, Database Hub in Fabric is now generally available. It provides a unified experience to discover, monitor, and manage databases across Azure, on-premises environments, and Fabric, with Fabric Copilot highlighting what needs attention. Read the latest Microsoft Databases announcements in this blog Turn ideas into governed enterprise-ready apps with Fabric apps, now generally available Great ideas for apps come from every corner of the business, and with Copilot, people can build one in minutes. But taking it from prototype to production on trusted data remains the biggest hurdle. Fabric apps, now generally available, bring together the backend services applications need with direct access to trusted data in Fabric, built-in security, and enterprise governance. Developers and coding agents build in code with open-source tools, and Fabric provisions everything from databases to authentication, with no infrastructure to manage. This makes it easier to turn ideas into enterprise-ready applications that can scale across the organization. ignite session: build like a startup… Watch now ↗ We’re also extending Fabric’s role as the data foundation for AI-powered applications. With the new Microsoft Copilot integration, now in Frontier public preview, anyone can describe the app they need and bring it to life, with the option to use Fabric as a ready-to-use data backend providing databases, storage, and data APIs. We’re also introducing Copilot Credits as a new usage-based billing option for Microsoft Fabric, providing greater flexibility alongside existing capacity-based options. Power BI creators can now build more than static reports. With a new agentic app creation experience in Power BI Desktop, now in preview, they can turn their existing semantic models into interactive apps that capture input, update data, and support operational workflows. Learn more about Fabric apps in the Ignite Microsoft Fabric blog Ground every agent in your business context with Microsoft IQ Most organizations already have the knowledge their agents need. It lives in the semantic models your analysts built in Power BI, the documents and procedures your teams rely on, the conversations happening across Microsoft 365, and the systems of record you run every day, like SAP and Oracle. The problem is that it’s scattered, so every new agent starts from zero and every team rebuilds the same context. That’s why we’re introducing Microsoft IQ, the enterprise context management platform for building your organization’s IQ. It brings together Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, Web IQ, and more than 350 connectors, so the knowledge your agents need is captured once, governed in one place, and reused by every agent and app. At the heart of Microsoft IQ are new business plugins, now available as part of the Frontier program. Business plugins turn what your teams know into trusted context, skills, and tools that anyone across the business can reuse. Take a supply chain disruption. A business plugin can tell an agent to use the components and orders semantic model in Fabric IQ to find the affected orders, the supplier contracts in Foundry IQ to check late-delivery terms, and Work IQ to find who owns the decision. Your domain experts write it once, and every agent across the organization inherits it. Teams can also reuse proven evaluations across agents instead of rebuilding them. The foundation underneath Microsoft IQ brings Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Fabric together in one path, built on Azure, to build, run, and continuously improve agents. And Agent 365 gives IT one place to observe, govern, and secure them. ignite session: Harnessing Your IQ… Watch now ↗ Your IQ stays yours, and it isn’t locked into one assistant. The same context and business plugins reach your agents wherever they run, in Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT, through model context protocol (MCP) and APIs. Your permissions and governance go with it. Agents can also draw on the business context in your systems of record, like SAP and Oracle, so they work from the data your teams already rely on. Learn more about Oracle’s latest integrations with Microsoft IQ. See how the Australian Energy Market Operator uses Microsoft IQ to help keep Australia’s power grid secure: Nearly 60,000 customers already use Microsoft IQ today. And because every agent builds on the same context, each one you add makes the next one better. Learn more about Microsoft IQ in this blog Experience these innovations at Microsoft Ignite Every agent you build is only as good as what it knows about your business. That’s why we’re making sure your IQ, the context that makes your company unique, is available to your agents across every layer of Azure, with governance and security built in. It stays yours, and its value grows with everything you build on it. To learn more about Microsoft IQ, I encourage you to join my Microsoft Ignite session, “Harnessing Your IQ with a continuously improving agent platform,” in person or online at no cost, or watch the recording afterward. For a closer look at all the innovation we are bringing to Azure, explore the full list of sessions on the Microsoft Ignite session catalog. title: [Docker] The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance
summary: The Agent Trust Gap The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt. It can execute code, access files, connect to services, and call external tools. That creates a new security question for enterprises: how do you give an agent enough freedom to be useful without giving it more access than it actually needs? A model decision is not automatically an authorized action. That distinction becomes important the moment an agent can turn a model output into an action in a real system. The answer can’t rely only on the model. Agent behavior can vary, while security controls need to be clear and enforceable. That means putting controls around the environment where the agent runs, what it can access, which tools it can use, and what happens when a policy allows or blocks an action. For a CISO, this creates a trust gap. Approving the use of AI agents means being able to answer more than whether the model is capable: what access does the agent have, where are those boundaries enforced, and what evidence is available afterward? The goal is to let teams adopt agents without making model behavior itself the security boundary. Docker AI Governance approaches this through three areas: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility. Together, they address three practical questions security teams need answered: Where can the agent operate? What can it do? And can we see what happened? In this article, I use “trust layer” as shorthand for the infrastructure between what an agent wants to do and what the organization actually allows it to do. There is a related trust question too: what software artifacts are these agentic workflows building and using? Docker Hardened Images address that software supply-chain side of the problem, alongside the runtime controls discussed below. Figure 1: The three layers of Docker AI Governance: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility. Sandbox Policies: Where Can the Agent Operate? An agent needs enough access to get real work done. A coding agent may need to install packages, build containers, edit project files, or connect to external services. The security challenge is deciding where those actions are allowed before the agent starts taking them. Docker Sandboxes give each agent an isolated microVM environment a lightweight virtual machine with its own Docker Engine, filesystem, and network. Docker AI Governance adds policy around that environment so security teams can control network and filesystem access centrally. Network policies can allow or block specific domains, IP ranges, and ports. Filesystem policies control which host paths can be mounted into a sandbox and whether that access is read-only or read-write. These controls are enforced at the network proxy and filesystem mount layers rather than depending on the agent to follow an instruction. For an organization, that means the same boundaries can follow developers across their sandboxes instead of being configured differently on every machine. Teams still get the access they need for their work, but an individual agent cannot simply expand those boundaries on its own. A developer can check the effective boundary before starting the agent: $ sbx policy check network api.anthropic.com Allowed: api.anthropic.com $ sbx policy check network blocked.example.com Denied: blocked.example.com The important part is that the result comes from the active policy, not from an instruction the agent is expected to follow. This answers the first governance question: Where can the agent operate? MCP Tool Governance: What Can the Agent Do? Once an agent has a controlled place to run, the next question is what it should be allowed to do through external tools. MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives agents a common way to connect to external tools, services, and capabilities, but that also expands what an agent can act on. For enterprise use, making a tool available should not automatically mean every agent can use it. Docker AI Governance puts policy around MCP activity handled through Docker’s MCP Gateway. Administrators can control which MCP servers may be registered and what agents can do through them, including tool calls, resources, prompts, and approval requirements. These organization policies are written in Cedar, a policy language used to express authorization rules. When MCP policy enforcement is active, governed requests are denied unless a matching policy permits them. For example, a policy can permit read-only tool calls for a specific registered MCP server: permit (principal, action == MCP::Action::"invokeTool", resource) when { resource in MCP::Server::"example" && resource.readOnly == true }; Here, readOnly comes from the MCP tool’s annotations. Those annotations are supplied by the server and are advisory, so this example relies on metadata provided by that server. This makes tool access an explicit policy decision rather than something left to each agent or developer to configure independently. A team can be given access to the tools it needs, while other servers or actions remain unavailable. Policies can also require confirmation for specific tool calls when an action needs an additional checkpoint. One boundary is worth making clear: MCP policies apply to activity handled by Docker’s MCP Gateway. If an agent connects directly to a remote MCP server from inside a sandbox, that connection falls under the sandbox’s network policy instead. With the environment constrained and tool access governed, we can answer the second question: What can the agent do? Audit + Visibility: Can We See What Happened? Setting a policy is only part of the job. Security teams also need to know when that policy was applied, what action triggered it, and whether the action was allowed or denied. Docker AI Governance records sandbox policy decisions and sandbox session events as structured audit records. Each record captures details such as the principal, action, target, decision, and time. The records contain governance metadata rather than the contents of prompts or agent responses. Audit records can be kept locally or delivered to the cloud. With cloud delivery enabled, teams can search the organization-wide record, export it for further analysis, or forward events into existing SIEM (security information and event management) workflows. Denied actions are especially useful. A team can see not only that an action failed, but that a governance rule blocked it and why. Allowed decisions matter too: they provide a record of how policy was applied while the agent was working. Current audit coverage includes Docker Sandboxes policy decisions and sandbox session events. The same schema can support additional Docker AI sources as they become available. That closes the third part of the governance loop: Can we see what happened? A Trusted Software Supply Chain: Docker Hardened Images AI Governance controls access around the agent at runtime. There is a separate question that matters to the workflows those agents participate in: what container images and software artifacts are they building, testing, or deploying? Docker Hardened Images provide minimal, secure, and production-ready container images, Helm charts, and system packages maintained by Docker. In practical terms, this gives teams evidence about what is inside an image and how that image was produced. Docker Hardened Images include signed SBOMs, VEX information, cryptographic signatures, and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. Instead of simply trusting where an image came from, teams can inspect what is inside it and verify information about how it was built. For organizations with additional compliance requirements, Docker also provides FIPS-enabled and STIG-ready variants through relevant DHI offerings. These capabilities sit alongside the broader DHI security and supply-chain controls rather than making any single standard the foundation by itself. AI Governance and Docker Hardened Images solve different parts of the trust problem. Governance controls the authority an agent has while it works; DHI helps establish trust in the container artifacts that the workflow depends on. Figure 2: Docker Hardened Images combine minimal container images with signed supply-chain metadata and verifiable build provenance. Putting the Three Layers Together Consider a developer using a coding agent to investigate an issue, update a service, and use an approved internal tool along the way. The agent begins inside a Docker Sandbox. It can work with the project and run the commands needed for the task, but its access is still bounded by policy. If it tries to reach a network destination or mount a host path that the organization has not allowed, the applicable sandbox policy can block that access. Now suppose the agent needs an MCP tool to look up information from another service. The request goes through Docker’s MCP Gateway, where organization policy determines whether that server and tool are permitted. A routine lookup might be allowed, while a more sensitive tool call could require confirmation or remain unavailable altogether. For governance activity currently covered by AI Governance Audit Logs, Docker records the policy decision and relevant session metadata. Security teams can see who initiated the activity, what policy-controlled action was evaluated, and whether it was allowed or denied. Those records can then feed the organization’s existing monitoring and SIEM workflow. If that same agent builds or tests a containerized application, the software entering the workflow matters too. Docker Hardened Images provide a more verifiable software foundation for that workflow, while AI Governance controls what the agent is authorized to do at runtime. The model is still making decisions about how to complete the task. What changes is the authority around those decisions. The agent can work autonomously inside the boundaries the organization has defined, while access outside those boundaries remains a policy decision. That is the practical value of the three layers working together: Sandbox Policies define where the agent can operate. MCP Tool Governance defines what tools it can use. Audit + Visibility shows how governed activity was handled. Taken together, the pattern is straightforward: define the boundary, check it before the agent starts working, enforce it while the agent is running, and use the resulting audit trail to understand what happened. If a boundary needs to change, the policy changes, not the expectation that the model will simply behave differently. Autonomy Without Unbounded Authority The challenge with agentic AI is not simply that agents can make decisions. It is that those decisions can now lead directly to actions. That makes the boundary around the agent just as important as the model itself. Docker AI Governance addresses that boundary through Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility: controlling where agents can operate, what tools they can use, and how governed activity is recorded. Docker Hardened Images address a related supply-chain concern by helping teams work with smaller, verifiable container artifacts. The goal is not to remove autonomy from agents. It is to make sure autonomy does not automatically come with unlimited authority. As agents take on more real work, that distinction will matter more and more.
